Stem
stĕm
n. (the stock or trunk of a tree, especially one cut down)
From the Saxon stemn, a stock or trunk. The Hebrew geza means a stump — what is left standing when a tree has been felled. It occurs once in this form, and it carries the Messianic promise of Isaiah 11.

Biblical Definition

One verse holds the word, and it is among the greatest in the prophets: “And there shall come forth a rod out of the stem of Jesse, and a Branch shall grow out of his roots” (Isaiah 11:1). The force of the sentence is in the word stem. It is not a tree; it is a stump. The house of David, by the time Isaiah has finished with Ahaz, is a felled thing — cut down to the ground, its royal line reduced to a stub in the soil, and named here not by the king's name but by his father's, Jesse of Bethlehem, as though the monarchy were being taken back to the farm it came from. Out of that stump a shoot comes. What rests on the shoot is stated next: “And the spirit of the LORD shall rest upon him, the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and might, the spirit of knowledge and of the fear of the LORD” (Isaiah 11:2). The reach of His kingdom follows: “And in that day there shall be a root of Jesse, which shall stand for an ensign of the people; to it shall the Gentiles seek: and his rest shall be glorious” (Isaiah 11:10). Paul cites that very line as the warrant for the Gentile mission: “And again, Esaias saith, There shall be a root of Jesse, and he that shall rise to reign over the Gentiles; in him shall the Gentiles trust” (Romans 15:12).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines stem as the principal body of a tree, shrub or plant; the stock; the race or family.

expand to see more

STEM, n. [Sax. stemn.] The principal body of a tree, shrub or plant; the stock; the firm part which supports the branches.

STEM, n. The stock of a family; race; generation; as, a noble stem.

ROD, n. A twig or shoot; a branch; also, an instrument of correction, and a badge of authority.

BRANCH, n. The shoot of a tree; in Scripture, an appellation of the Messiah, Isaiah 11:1; Jeremiah 23:5.

ENSIGN, n. The flag or banner of a military band; a standard set up as a signal of gathering.

Key Scripture

Isaiah 11:1 — "And there shall come forth a rod out of the stem of Jesse, and a Branch shall grow out of his roots:"

Isaiah 11:2 — "And the spirit of the LORD shall rest upon him, the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and might, the spirit of knowledge and of the fear of the LORD;"

Isaiah 11:10 — "And in that day there shall be a root of Jesse, which shall stand for an ensign of the people; to it shall the Gentiles seek: and his rest shall be glorious."

Romans 15:12 — "And again, Esaias saith, There shall be a root of Jesse, and he that shall rise to reign over the Gentiles; in him shall the Gentiles trust."

Modern Corruption

The prophecy is reassigned to a purely eighth-century hope for a better Judean king, and the stump is turned into a metaphor for national resilience.

expand to see more

The historical-critical reading confines Isaiah 11 to its own century: the prophet hopes for a righteous Davidic successor, perhaps Hezekiah, and the language is court rhetoric of a familiar Near Eastern kind. The dictionary rejects this reading and follows the apostle. Paul quotes verse 10 in Romans 15:12 as a prophecy of Christ's reign over the Gentiles, and the New Testament's use of the Old is the authoritative use. A prophecy that terminates on Hezekiah cannot bear the weight of verses 6 through 9, and no Judean king ever did.

A softer corruption preaches the stump as a lesson in resilience — nations and people can be cut down and still come back. The text says the opposite about the stump. A stump cannot come back; that is what makes it a stump. The whole point of naming Jesse rather than David is that the royal house had been reduced to the obscurity it started in, and that nothing in the wood accounts for the shoot. The rod comes forth because God promised it would, and the Spirit rests on Him because the Father gives Him the Spirit without measure. The doctrine is sovereign grace, not natural recovery.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew geza (H1503), a stump or stock; choter (H2415), a rod or shoot; netser (H5342), a branch or sprout; shoresh (H8328), a root.

expand to see more

Hebrew geza (H1503) — the stump of a felled tree; Isaiah 11:1, the stem of Jesse.

Hebrew choter (H2415) — a twig, rod, shoot; that which comes forth from the stump.

Hebrew netser (H5342) — a green shoot, Branch; a Messianic title in Isaiah 11:1.

Hebrew shoresh (H8328) — a root; Isaiah 11:10, a root of Jesse for an ensign.

Hebrew nes (H5251) — a standard, ensign, banner lifted for the nations to see.

Usage

"“A rod out of the stem of Jesse” — a shoot from a felled house."

"“The spirit of the LORD shall rest upon him” — the anointing of the shoot."

"“To it shall the Gentiles seek” — the reach Paul claims for the gospel."
